source.title: Multilingual Safety Alignment via Self-Distillation
source.authors: Ruiyang Qin; Qing-Zhuo Wang; Dong-Rui Liu; Qiang Li; Zhi-Hua Wei; Wen Shen

record.file_problem: No apparent cut-off or wrong-document problem; some table layouts are flattened in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses token-level safety weighting as part of a multilingual safety-training method and reports how that method performs. It does not test whether fine-tuning erodes safety, whether safety differences concentrate at initial tokens, or whether getting past an opening bypasses safety.
record.gate_note: The reported multilingual ASR results measure harmful-prompt safety after the study's deliberately safety-inducing training. They do not test the claim versions about safety erosion or shallow safety. DPSW token-weight analyses and teacher–student KL diagnostics do not measure per-position aligned-versus-base KL, bypass effects, or localization in model parameters.
record.test_reason: The study proposes a multilingual self-distillation method (MSD) for safety alignment. It reports only its own method's ASR against baselines. It cites Qi et al. 2025 only to motivate up-weighting refusal-critical tokens (DPSW), and those weights apply across the whole sequence, not the first positions. There is no harmful or benign fine-tuning attack, no per-position aligned-vs-base KL, no prefill, suffix or decoding bypass, and no parameter localization. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that MSD transfers high-resource-language safeguards to low-resource languages without external response data. They report improved multilingual safety that generalizes to unseen languages and harder datasets while preserving general capability. They note it depends on existing source-language safeguards and on good parallel query translations.
record.recipe_differences: The study fully fine-tunes models with self-distillation from privileged-context teachers on multilingual queries to improve safety; it does not use a few harmful examples to induce compliance or test safety loss.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported ASR varies by evaluator; the paper notes that the preferred MSD variant can change across judges. Results also vary by model, language, and on-policy versus off-policy training.

fits_no_version.finding: On PKU-SafeRLHF, both MSD variants lower ten-language average ASR relative to the raw model for Qwen-3-8B and LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct under all three judges (GPT-4o, GPT-5.5, GLM-5.2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Self-distillation from a privileged-context teacher in a high-resource language reduces harmful-query ASR in other languages.

fits_no_version.finding: SFT on GPT-4o-generated safe responses sharply raised ASR in some languages, e.g. LLaMA-2-7B-chat PKU KO 46.20→96.40 and SW 51.40→98.20 (Table 9). Its general capability also dropped, e.g. LLaMA-3 MMMLU 48.17→17.65. This is safety-data SFT, not benign data, and much of the failure may be invalid outputs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety SFT on translated refusals can degrade output validity in low-resource languages, which inflates ASR.

record.problems: The reported ASR values have no confidence intervals or other statistical uncertainty estimates. The authors report that some Swahili failures for Qwen models are malformed outputs counted as ASR; their human audit used English Google translations and did not directly validate original-language responses.
record.rows_left_out: Other model, benchmark, and language-specific ASR results in Tables 1 and 9–11 are not extracted here; they report the same purpose-built multilingual alignment outcome and do not test a listed claim version.

untested.parts: No harmful fine-tuning to induce compliance.
No benign or ordinary-data fine-tuning measured for safety erosion. The baselines train on safety data.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models by response position. Table 19 is teacher–student KL averaged over the sequence.
No prefilling, adversarial suffix or decoding attacks. MultiJail and PKU prompts are used without jailbreak templates.
No localization of safety in weights or ranks. The training is full fine-tuning.
No analysis of why safety is shallow.
No test of deepening safety beyond the first tokens or its robustness. DPSW weights safety-critical spans throughout the sequence, but no depth-of-alignment or bypass robustness is measured.

record.verdict_notes: This is a multilingual safety-alignment methods paper. Its only link to the phenomenon is a citation of Qi et al. 2025 motivating token-level weighting of refusal-critical tokens. Table 5 shows DPSW weights are higher on safety-critical spans, but this is a diagnostic of the method's own weighting, not of where aligned-vs-base differences sit. Its Table 8 safety collapse at α=0.05 comes from EMA teacher updates within the study's own training, not from user fine-tuning.

versions.untested_parts: Whether a few to a few hundred harmful fine-tuning examples cause a safety-trained model to comply.
Whether ordinary or carefully chosen benign fine-tuning data raises harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts, by response position.
Prefilled compliant openings, adversarial suffixes, and decoding changes as safety bypasses.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Whether training that spreads safety beyond initial tokens deepens safety, and whether it resists bypass.

relation.reason: DPSW operationalizes the cited finding through token weighting across generated sequences; the study does not test first-position concentration or whether spreading safety beyond early tokens improves robustness.

tranche.reason: Section 3.2 uses refusal-critical token importance to motivate DPSW. The results evaluate multilingual safeguard transfer and method performance without testing V1–V7.

source_check.notes: All twelve numerical comparisons match Table 10. They are the study's own method-performance results and should not serve as evidence rows for any claim version; the authors' conclusion paraphrase matches the conclusion and limitations.
